extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary friends, and editors (e.g., Coleridge, Southey) interested in poetic composition and criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance and compositional advice for poets (especially Romantic-era verse): how to choose subject, tone, diction, form, and keep proportion between matter and style. Includes practical notes on printing/selection and examples of anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion between matter and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid a 'faulty disproportion in the matter and the style' — the material of a poem must suit the stylistic manner in which it is treated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb objects where lofty, solemn openings are followed by incongruous low, domestic scenes (e.g., a 'publican's daughter' episode after sublime preluding strains): 'The texture will be most lamentably disproportionate.' If you perceive no disproportion, all argument is vain; but if there is, it mars the whole effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity in delineating common and natural feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Delineations of common and natural feelings should aim for simplicity rather than artifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb praises 'simplicity' for familiar walks of poetry and warns against artificial turns: 'I hate made-dishes at the muses' banquet.' Keep expressions natural and avoid affected phrases when treating ordinary emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of mood and subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain consistency between the poem's mood/ambition and its incidents or additions; don't intermingle vastly different registers without care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticizes inserting 'cock-and-a-bull' domestic episodes into high-minded pieces (e.g., Joan of Arc). Advice: 'Leave the lowlands, unenvied, in possession of such men as Cowper and Southey' — let each passage remain in its proper region of tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and versification — avoid monotony
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure rhythmic vitality; avoid 'utter want of all rhythm,' monotony, and 'dead plumb-down of the pauses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb echoes Coleridge's later critique of certain lines: monotony and absence of rhythm are serious blemishes. Versification should suit the thought and sustain musical interest throughout: 'The versification is throughout, to my ears, unexceptionable' when it matches the ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highly finished emotional description for prophet/fanatic figures
rubrics_metrics.description: When portraying a fanatic or prophetic figure (e.g., Joan), the description of their emotions should be especially polished and finished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb: 'in an account of a fanatic or of a prophet the description of her emotions is expected to be most highly finished.' Attention to subtle gradations of feeling is required in such portraits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ludicrous or inappropriate phrases that diminish effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from lines or turns of phrase that unintentionally lessen the intended emotional or dramatic impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives examples as anti-patterns: 'hailed him immortal' (ludicrous), 'voiced a sad and simple tale' (abominable), and 'unprovendered' — such phrases can undercut terror, solemnity, or pathos and should be revised or omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity in characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer particular, concrete character details to vague generalities about a life or experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of saying 'his eventful years all come and gone' make the character specific (e.g., 'make him a soldier') so the reader can imagine concrete scenes and the emotion becomes more palpable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate word choice and diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose words that accurately fit the feeling and register intended; beware of incongruous or clumsy vocabulary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: prefer 'troublous' to 'turbid ecstasy' — 'turbid' suggests muddy inspiration (London porter) and misfits the grandeur. Lamb repeatedly flags single-word misfits that jar the reader and recommends precise, fitting synonyms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match metrical measure to thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a metrical form that is 'fitted to the thoughts' you express; the measure should complement the ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb praises the metrical fit of Coleridge's 'Religious Musings' as 'exactly fitted to the thoughts.' Poor matches between meter and content produce awkwardness or diminish force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contrived poetic artifices ('made-dishes')
rubrics_metrics.description: Steer clear of contrivances and overly composed artifices that feel cooked-up rather than organically arising from feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb's metaphor: 'I hate made-dishes at the muses' banquet.' Anti-patterns include artificial verbal turns or set-piece effects that don't proceed naturally from emotion or situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve simplicity in familiar narrative lines
rubrics_metrics.description: When working in familiar or anecdotal modes (the 'familiar walks of poetry'), simplicity and plain telling often work better than ornate phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts the 'plain tale' telling (Cowper, Southey) with attempts at ambitious ornament in domestic or homely scenes. If aiming for plain narrative, avoid overwriting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and presentation of sonnets — fidelity and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: When preparing sonnets for print, prefer to print them 'verbatim' and avoid including potentially ambiguous lines that can be misread (e.g., allusions that look like references to living persons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb requests: 'I need not repeat my wishes to have my little sonnets printed verbatim... I fear lest you should prefer printing my first sonnet, as you have done more than once, "did the wand of Merlin wave," it looks so like Mr. Merlin... one half who read it would understand it so.' Practical editorial note: respect authorial intent and be wary of lines that invite unintended readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: A grand aim (e.g., the epic) concentrates poetic faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Committing to a large, definitive work (like an epic) can focus and fully develop a poet's talents and ambition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb urges Coleridge: 'I adjure you to attempt the epic... Having one great end to direct all your poetical faculties to... your ambition will show you to what you are equal.' Advice for career-shaping: choose a single large project to concentrate effort and reach high accomplishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty about originality and personal purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Be candid about whether a piece is original or merely personal/memorial; personal motives can justify inclusion even when not highly original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb admits some lines 'have no originality in its cast' yet defends printing them because they serve as 'perpetuating tokens of my affection.' Not every line must be novel—personal function and sincerity can be legitimate reasons to keep material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of rivalry and audience comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious when writing in territories populated by admired contemporaries—the work will invite comparison and may be disadvantaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb warns that Coleridge's imitation of Southey's 'fierce and terrible benevolence' may 'look like rivalship' and 'extort a comparison' which could injure reception. Consider whether to avoid direct overlap with another poet's signature strengths.
